ai.literal: Than those who have undertaken murder, more cruel indeed is the king who, having undertaken harassment, conducts himself doing unjust things.
ai.translation: More cruel than those who make a living by murder is the king who oppresses his subjects and rules with injustice.
ai.modern: கொலை செய்வதைத் தொழிலாகக் கொண்டவர்களை விட, தன் குடிமக்களைத் துன்புறுத்தி அறமல்லாத செயல்களைச் செய்து வாழும் அரசன் மிகவும் கொடியவன் ஆவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares a tyrannical ruler to murderers. The poet states that a king who oppresses his subjects ('அலை மேற்கொண்டு') and acts unjustly ('அல்லவை செய்து') is far more cruel ('கொடிதே') than those who commit murder ('கொலை மேற்கொண்டார்'). While murderers kill individuals, an unjust ruler destroys the livelihood and peace of an entire nation. The key words 'அலை' (harassment/oppression) and 'அல்லவை' (unjust deeds) highlight the destructive nature of bad governance.

ai.literal: Like a robber standing with a spear saying 'Give!', is the demanding of a ruler standing with a sceptre.
ai.translation: A ruler demanding wealth from his subjects while holding the sceptre of power is just like a highway robber standing with a spear and demanding, 'Hand over your wealth!'
ai.modern: செங்கோலை ஏந்தி நிற்கும் அரசன் தன் குடிமக்களிடம் வரி கொடுக்குமாறு இரந்து கேட்பது, கையில் வேலை ஏந்தி வழியில் நிற்பவன் 'உன் பொருளைக் கொடு' என்று மிரட்டுவதைப் போன்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares a tyrannical ruler's unjust demands for money to highway robbery. The sceptre (கோல்) is meant to be a symbol of protection and justice, but when used to extort wealth, it functions exactly like a robber's spear (வேல்). The word 'இரவு' in this context refers to the ruler's demand or begging for extra taxes from his helpless subjects. The comparison vividly illustrates that state extortion under the guise of law is nothing but armed banditry.

ai.literal: Every day, having investigated, justice not-administering king's, every day the country will be ruined.
ai.translation: The country of a king who does not investigate and administer justice daily will ruin itself day by day.
ai.modern: நாள்தோறும் ஆராய்ந்து நீதி வழங்காத அரசனுடைய நாடானது, நாள்தோறும் அழிவை நோக்கிச் செல்லும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the immediate and continuous consequences of negligent governance. The poet uses the word 'நாடொறும்' (every day) twice to establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. If a ruler fails to investigate grievances ('நாடி') and deliver justice ('முறைசெய்யா') on a daily basis, the decline of the nation is not a distant event but a daily process of decay ('நாடு கெடும்'). Good governance requires constant vigilance, and its absence leads to the steady, day-by-day ruin of the state.

ai.literal: Wealth and subjects together will lose, sceptre having bent, without deliberating, the king who acts.
ai.translation: A ruler who acts without deliberation, bending the sceptre of justice, will lose both his wealth and his subjects at once.
ai.modern: நீதிநெறி தவறி, ஆராய்ந்து பார்க்காமல் காரியங்களைச் செய்யும் அரசன், தன் செல்வத்தையும் தன் குடிமக்களையும் ஒருசேர இழப்பான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the dual ruin that awaits a tyrant. The phrase 'கோல்கோடி' (bending the sceptre) represents the deviation from justice, while 'சூழாது செய்யும்' describes a ruler who acts impulsively without proper deliberation or counsel. Such a ruler will simultaneously lose 'கூழும்' (the state's wealth and resources) and 'குடியும்' (the loyalty and presence of the subjects), leading to the complete collapse of the kingdom.

ai.literal: Suffering having experienced, unable to bear, wept tears indeed, wealth wearing away weapon.
ai.translation: The tears shed by subjects who suffer and cannot bear the cruelty of a tyrant are indeed the weapon that wears away his wealth.
ai.modern: கொடுங்கோன்மையால் துன்பப்பட்டு, அதனைப் பொறுக்க முடியாமல் அழுத மக்களின் கண்ணீர்தான், ஒரு மன்னனின் செல்வத்தை அழிக்கும் ஆயுதமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the silent but destructive power of the tears of oppressed subjects. When people suffer under a tyrant and find their misery unbearable ('ஆற்றாது'), they weep in despair. The tears ('கண்ணீர்') they shed are not merely signs of grief; they act as a powerful weapon ('படை') that gradually erodes and destroys the ruler's prosperity and power ('செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும்'). The word 'அன்றே' emphasizes that this destruction is certain and inevitable, showing that a ruler's oppression contains the very seeds of his own ruin.

ai.literal: To kings, permanence is just governance; if that is not there, not enduring will become to kings the glory.
ai.translation: For kings, permanence of rule comes from a just sceptre; if that is lacking, their glory will not endure.
ai.modern: மன்னர்களுக்கு நிலைத்தன்மை தருவது நேர்மையான ஆட்சிமுறை ஆகும்; அது இல்லாவிட்டால், மன்னர்களுடைய புகழானது நிலைபெறாமல் அழியும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that the stability of a king's reign depends entirely on just governance (செங்கோன்மை). The word 'மன்னுதல்' means enduring or remaining stable. If a ruler lacks a just sceptre, their 'ஒளி' (glory or fame) will not last ('மன்னாவாம்'). Thus, the poet emphasizes that justice is the sole foundation of a ruler's lasting reputation and authority.

ai.literal: The absence of rain drops to the world of what nature, like that indeed is the king's absence of grace to the living beings.
ai.translation: Just as the absence of rain brings ruin to the world, so does the absence of a king's grace bring misery to his subjects.
ai.modern: மழைத்துளி இல்லாதிருப்பது உலகத்திற்கு எவ்வளவு துன்பமோ, அதுபோலவே அரசனுடைய அருள் இல்லாதிருப்பது அவனுடைய நாட்டில் வாழும் உயிர்களுக்குத் துன்பமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the vital necessity of a ruler's grace to the necessity of rain for the world. The word 'துளி' refers to rain drops, representing the life-giving water that sustains all earthly existence. 'அளி' means grace, compassion, or benevolence, which is the essential quality a ruler must possess to protect their subjects. Just as the 'இன்மை' (absence) of rain causes the physical world to wither and perish, the 'இன்மை' (absence) of a king's compassion causes the 'வாழும் உயிர்க்கு' (living beings) under his rule to suffer and decline.

ai.literal: Than poverty, is more painful possession of wealth, if one falls under the scepter of a king who does not do justice.
ai.translation: If one must live under the scepter of a king who does not administer justice, possessing wealth is far more painful than suffering poverty.
ai.modern: நீதி செலுத்தாத அரசனுடைய செங்கோல் ஆட்சியின்கீழ் வாழ நேர்ந்தால், வறுமையை விடச் செல்வத்தை உடையவராக இருப்பது அதிகத் துன்பத்தைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the dread of living under an unjust ruler. The poet states that if a person lives under a king who does not deliver justice ('முறை செய்யா மன்னவன்'), having wealth ('உடைமை') becomes a greater source of misery than poverty ('இன்மை'). Under a tyrannical regime, the wealthy are constantly targeted, extorted, or harassed, making their possessions a liability. Thus, the pain of holding wealth under tyranny far exceeds the hardships of having nothing at all.

ai.literal: If the king does rule having swerved from justice, the rain having swerved, the sky will not agree to rain.
ai.translation: If a king rules deviating from the path of justice, the clouds will swerve from their seasonal cycle and the sky will refuse to yield rain.
ai.modern: மன்னன் நீதி தவறி ஆட்சி செய்வானானால், மேகம் தன் பருவம் தப்பி மழை பொழிதலைச் செய்யாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the classical belief that a ruler's moral conduct directly influences the natural world. The word 'muṟai' refers to the straight path of justice, while 'kōṭi' means to bend or deviate. If the king bends justice, the rain ('uṟai') will also bend away from its regular season. Consequently, the sky ('vāṉam') will refuse ('ollātu') to perform its duty of raining ('peyal'), leading to drought and famine.

ai.literal: Cow's yield will diminish; those of six duties their sacred books will forget, if the protector does not protect.
ai.translation: If the guardian king fails to protect his subjects, the yield of cows will diminish, and those of the six duties will forget their sacred learning.
ai.modern: நாட்டைக் காக்கும் அரசன் தன் குடிமக்களைக் காப்பாற்றவில்லை என்றால், பசுக்கள் தரும் பால் வளம் குறையும்; அறநெறி சார்ந்த ஆறு தொழில்களைச் செய்யும் அந்தணர்கள் தங்கள் வேத நூல்களை மறந்துவிடுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the total collapse of societal order and prosperity under a ruler who fails to protect his people. The 'yield of cows' (ஆபயன்) represents the material wealth and agricultural abundance of the land, which declines when there is no security. 'Those of the six duties' (அறுதொழிலோர்) refers to the learned class responsible for maintaining wisdom and rituals; without royal protection, they lose the peace required to preserve their sacred texts (நூல்). Thus, a king's failure to protect (காவான் எனின்) destroys both the physical sustenance and the intellectual-spiritual foundation of his kingdom.
